quiz.question: Why do web applications use session identifiers?
options: To encrypt every HTTP request automatically
To associate requests with an application session and its authentication state
To replace all backend authorization checks
To prove that every request is safe
quiz.explanation: HTTP is a stateless protocol (RFC 9110). A session identifier allows the backend to bind subsequent requests from a browser to an established authenticated state in the database or session store.

quiz.question: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute do?
options: Prevents the browser from ever sending the cookie
Encrypts the cookie value
Prevents ordinary JavaScript APIs from reading the cookie directly
Eliminates the need for session expiration
quiz.explanation: The HttpOnly flag instructs the browser that the cookie should not be accessible via client-side scripts like document.cookie, mitigating direct credential extraction during XSS attacks.

quiz.question: What is the same-origin policy designed to do?
options: Restrict certain cross-origin script interactions in the browser
Authenticate every user to every API
Encrypt all website data at rest
Replace server-side authorization
quiz.explanation: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) is a foundational browser security control that isolates documents and scripts loaded from different origins (scheme, host, and port) to prevent malicious sites from reading confidential data from other sites.

quiz.question: What is the correct relationship between CORS and backend authorization?
options: CORS makes backend authorization unnecessary
CORS controls browser cross-origin response access; backend authorization must still be enforced
CORS is an alternative to HTTPS
CORS guarantees that requests cannot be sent cross-origin
quiz.explanation: CORS is purely a browser-enforced mechanism governing whether JavaScript can read a cross-origin response. The server still receives and processes the request, meaning robust server-side authentication and authorization must always be enforced.

quiz.question: Which is a key defense against CSRF in a stateful web application?
options: Allow state-changing actions through GET requests
Hide all buttons that change application state
Use appropriate request-intent validation such as CSRF tokens, supported by suitable cookie and origin policies
Disable authentication for API endpoints
quiz.explanation: CSRF defenses require validating user intent via unpredictable anti-CSRF synchronizer tokens, verified SameSite cookies (Lax or Strict), Origin/Referer headers, and ensuring state-changing actions never use safe GET methods.

quiz.question: Why is Content Security Policy useful?
options: It restricts permitted browser resource behavior and can reduce the impact of some XSS attacks
It eliminates every type of XSS vulnerability
It automatically proves that the user is authorized
It replaces all cookie security attributes
quiz.explanation: Content Security Policy (CSP) provides defense in depth by restricting which scripts, styles, frames, and connections the browser can execute, dramatically mitigating the impact of XSS and clickjacking.

theorySections.title: Web Application Architecture and Request Lifecycle
paragraphs: A modern web application is an orchestrated ecosystem consisting of client browsers, frontend JavaScript runtimes, reverse proxies or API gateways, backend services, relational or NoSQL databases, identity providers (IdPs), and third-party SaaS integrations.

{`[ USER BROWSER ] ◄── Uncontrolled Environment (DOM, LocalStorage, DevTools) │ ▲ │ │ HTTPS + Cookies + SOP / CORS / CSP Enforced by Browser ▼ │ [ REVERSE PROXY / API GATEWAY ] ◄── Edge Trust Boundary (TLS Termination, WAF, Rate Limits) │ ▲ │ │ Internal Network / Mutual TLS (mTLS) ▼ │ [ BACKEND APPLICATION ] ◄── Core Authorization Boundary (RBAC/ABAC, Session Validation) │ ▲ │ │ Database Queries (Parameterized SQL / ORM) ▼ │ [ DATABASE & IDENTITY PROVIDER ] ◄── Data & Auth Anchors (Persistent State, Token Signer)`} Safe Methods (RFC 9110) GET and HEAD are defined as safe and idempotent. They must never trigger state changes, database writes, or financial transactions.
POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE require explicit authentication, object-level authorization, input validation, and anti-CSRF protections.

theorySections.title: HTTP Sessions, Session Fixation, and Lifecycle Management
paragraphs: Because HTTP is inherently stateless, applications construct stateful interactions using session identifiers. A session ID is a high-entropy bearer token that references a record stored in a secure server-side session cache (e.g., Redis).

An attacker establishes an anonymous session ID, feeds it to a victim (via URL parameter or phishing link), and waits for the victim to log in. If the application does NOT issue a fresh session ID upon login, the attacker uses the known session ID to access the victim's authenticated account!

Many developers simply clear the cookie on the browser side via JavaScript or an empty Set-Cookie header, but leave the session valid in the server Redis store. If an attacker stole the session token earlier, it remains fully usable until server expiration!

theorySections.title: Cookies, Cookie Security Flags, and Client-Side Storage
paragraphs: Cookies (RFC 6265) are automatically attached by browsers to matching requests. To prevent exploitation, developers must configure specific security flags.

Storing JWTs or API keys in localStorage is accessible to ANY JavaScript running on that origin. If an XSS vulnerability occurs (or a compromised npm dependency runs), the token is immediately exfiltrated.
Best Practice: Use HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax session cookies with a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) proxy to keep sensitive tokens entirely out of browser JavaScript memory.

theorySections.title: Same-Origin Policy (SOP), CORS, and Content Security Policy (CSP)
paragraphs: An Origin is strictly defined as the combination of Scheme + Host + Port. If any of the three differs, it is considered a different origin by the browser.
1. Wildcard with Credentials: Modern browsers forbid Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

2. Blind Origin Reflection: Naive servers take the incoming Origin header from the request and dynamically echo it back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. This effectively grants arbitrary external attacker websites complete access to authenticated API data!
